doc.title: Derek Brown interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 5, 2021

title: Tone of smooth jazz, rap and nostalgia for 80s-90s pop
summary: Rowe compares Cannonball Adderley; Brown on smooth-jazz tone, avoiding rap as a good kid, and his love of the pop backbeat on two and four.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Very significant. I did the same thing with Cannonball Adderley. Talking about filling the horn.
Like playing it from this end to that end.
Yeah. And also in the mid 80s the rap music started to become quite popular and I just wondered if that entered your consciousness. Because you’re so, you’re such a percussive guy.

I am yeah. It’s funny, well I didn’t always get into rap when I was younger mainly because my parents would not have approved. And I was very much a goody two shoes. You know I talked about wanting to please people, I really wanted to please my parents. It worked for me. I was happy that way, not kind of like stretching the boundaries when I was a kid, though we did listen to — I would often just say, just all the pop music we listened to, the 80s pop, 90s pop, where there’s always a backbeat on two and four, just such a universal thing. And you listen to my music nowadays almost always there’s a backbeat on two and four. I will never, until I die, I will never get sick of that. I love that. And it’s this thing that people say, like they’ve done studies on this, the music you listen to when you’re a teenager, it’s going to stay with you your whole life. And so it’s like it doesn’t matter how cheesy it seems nowadays, it’s nostalgic for me. When I hear that, like Bryan Adams, Tears for Fears, whatever that, heavy reverb on two and four, and those synths, it’s so nostalgic to me. It just like warms my heart in a way that, and I’ll be honest, in a way that a lot of jazz maybe doesn’t, just because I didn’t grow up with that during that time, and I think it has to do with when you’re a teenager your first kiss, first © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

dance, experiencing all these things, that’s the soundtrack of your growing up. And it’s like life is too short to like move beyond that. And I’ve learned to just embrace it. It’s okay. I like the stuff and it’s okay if this enters my playing. Yeah.
